item.title: Radrodro encourages Gavoka to work on delivering according to the wishes of SODELPA members and citizens of Fiji
item.description: SODELPA Leader, Aseri Radrodro stresses that as the Party Leader, like SODELPA MP, Viliame Gavoka, he is bound to the supreme authority of the party which is their general assembly and they had made their position clear during the party Special General Assembly. While responding to Gavoka's comments that he is devastated by the party’s stance that they will not support the vote for the Constitutio
item.content:encoded:
SODELPA Leader, Aseri Radrodro stresses that as the Party Leader, like SODELPA MP, Viliame Gavoka, he is bound to the supreme authority of the party which is their general assembly and they had made their position clear during the party Special General Assembly.

While responding to Gavoka's comments that he is devastated by the party’s stance that they will not support the vote for the Constitution Amendment Bill and the SODELPA MPs have to vote against the Bill in the final reading in Parliament on Monday, Radrodro says he will encourage Gavoka to utilize his unique position being a member of the Special Committee and lobby them on the pertinent issues that is stopping SODELPA from supporting the Bill in its current form.

Radrodro says Gavoka could be helpful that way and SODELPA will be grateful for his input to enable SODELPA to deliver according to the wishes of its members and citizens of Fiji who have publicly shared similar sentiments.

He says t his is a defining moment for Fiji that should unite us rather than divide or polarize us and SODELPA will always listen to the voices of the people.

Radrodro stresses this must not be an election promise exercise but must be one in which every citizen's voice is considered and our laws changed or improved and we all take ownership of it.

item.title: 11 days not enough for Fijians to understand proposed Constitution changes – Vuki
item.description: Ordinary Fijians cannot be expected to understand complex constitutional changes in just 11 days, and need more time to make informed submissions on proposals that could shape the country's future. This is the concern raised by Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission Commissioner Alefina Vuki, who says people need proper public education, clear explanations and sufficient time to unde
item.content:encoded:
Ordinary Fijians cannot be expected to understand complex constitutional changes in just 11 days, and need more time to make informed submissions on proposals that could shape the country's future.

This is the concern raised by Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission Commissioner Alefina Vuki, who says people need proper public education, clear explanations and sufficient time to understand the proposed amendments.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Vuki says the Constitution is a complex legal document, and people should not be expected to fully understand the proposed changes within such a short period.

She says the Government should provide public education on the 2013 Constitution, the Constitutional Review Commission's report, the proposed amendments and the Government's revised draft.

Vuki says people also need time to seek advice from teachers, doctors and others in their communities who can help explain the proposals.

She is calling for the documents to be translated into iTaukei and Hindi, while the English versions should be written in plain language to make them easier to understand.

Vuki stresses that people cannot make informed decisions if they do not understand what is being proposed.

She says the Commission supports amending the 2013 Constitution because it believes the document was imposed on the people.

However, Vuki says the Commission's main concern is not whether the Constitution should be changed, but how the changes are being carried out.

She says constitutional amendments require greater public consultation and accountability than ordinary laws because the Constitution is the country's highest law.

Vuki also questions the limited time allocated for public submissions, pointing out that only three hours were provided for submissions in Suva.

She says the Commission decided not to make an oral presentation because it wanted ordinary members of the public to have more time to express their views.

Instead, the Commission submitted its views in writing before the deadline.

Vuki says the Commission also needed sufficient time to assess the proposed changes against the nine international human rights conventions she says Fiji has ratified.

She explains that this includes examining whether the proposed Bill of Rights meets Fiji's international human rights commitments.

Vuki says such an assessment requires careful consideration and cannot be completed without sufficient time.

She also points to the process that led to the 1997 Constitution, saying the committee responsible took about 13 months to complete its work.

Vuki believes Fiji should learn from previous constitutional review processes and allow enough time for meaningful public participation.

She stresses that Fijians must be given a fair opportunity to understand the proposed changes, ask questions and make informed submissions before decisions are made about the country's Constitution.

item.title: More than 1,600 suspected marijuana plants discovered in Northern Division, police continue nationwide drug operations
item.description: Police say a farm containing more than 1,500 plants believed to be marijuana was discovered earlier this week in the Vesivuru farming area in Lea. In a separate operation, a team from Tukavesi conducting a mop-up exercise in the Nawi farming area discovered another farm containing more than 100 plants believed to be marijuana.
item.content:encoded:
Police say a farm containing more than 1,500 plants believed to be marijuana was discovered earlier this week in the Vesivuru farming area in Lea.

In a separate operation, a team from Tukavesi conducting a mop-up exercise in the Nawi farming area discovered another farm containing more than 100 plants believed to be marijuana.

Police say a 38-year-old man, believed to be the owner of the farm, was arrested and taken into custody.

The mop-up exercises involved revisiting areas known for drug cultivation and resulted in further seizures.

Meanwhile, in Labasa, Police say a hotel employee discovered white substances suspected to be illicit drugs in a hotel room.

The substances were handed over to Police and have been sent for analysis.

In the Western Division, a joint raid conducted by the Fiji Detector Dog Unit and Namaka Police resulted in the seizure of a large amount of cash believed to be proceeds of crime, along with equipment suspected to have been used in drug distribution.

Police say two men were also arrested at a residence in Sabeto as investigations continue.

In the Eastern Division, a man and a woman were arrested in Levuka for alleged unlawful possession of marijuana.

They also face an additional charge of allegedly resisting arrest.

In the Southern Division, a 19-year-old man was arrested along Gaji Road after he was allegedly found in possession of a zip-lock bag containing a white substance believed to be methamphetamine.

Meanwhile, Police are urging members of the public to immediately report any parcels suspected to contain illicit substances.

A parcel containing white substances was discovered yesterday along the seashore in Dakuinuku Village and handed over to Police.

Members of the public are encouraged to report suspicious activities by calling 1681 or sending photos and videos via WhatsApp or Viber to 9905922.

Police are also reminding people not to handle suspicious packages and to alert authorities as soon as possible.

item.title: May 2000 coup showed how quickly people can lose their sense of safety - Kiran
item.description: The violence and fear that followed the May 2000 coup showed how quickly people can lose their sense of safety when law and order break down. Speaking during the Fiji Truth and Reconciliation Commission hearing, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection, Sashi Kiran recalled how she learnt of the takeover on May 19th 2000, while working as a coordinator with the Fiji Council of Social Ser
item.content:encoded:
The violence and fear that followed the May 2000 coup showed how quickly people can lose their sense of safety when law and order break down.

Speaking during the Fiji Truth and Reconciliation Commission hearing, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection, Sashi Kiran recalled how she learnt of the takeover on May 19th 2000, while working as a coordinator with the Fiji Council of Social Services.

Kiran says she had been attending a regular business meeting when she contacted the then Assistant Minister for National Affairs to ask about the situation, as a march and civil unrest were expected.

She says she was reassured that everything was under control and there was no immediate cause for concern.

However, Kiran says the situation changed rapidly when a message arrived on her mobile phone reporting that people had taken over Parliament.

She says an event planned for that day was cancelled, and staff were quickly organised to return home.

By the time they left, parts of the city had descended into looting and violence, leaving people experiencing fear, pressure and anguish.

Kiran says people began reaching out for help the following day, with women and children who had been abused among those needing support.

She says her focus at the time was on helping victims rather than identifying the perpetrators.

Kiran recalled how families were forced from their homes and sought shelter with relatives and other communities, while some people who offered shelter were also attacked.

She says she still remembered seeing people in tears, asking for help to remove their belongings from homes they feared they would be forced to leave.

Kiran says the experience raised serious questions about what could be done when people could no longer rely on the usual systems for protection.

Reflecting on the events, she says the crisis also highlighted the impact of political leaders’ words and the need to take public anger and concerns seriously before tensions escalate.

Kiran says there had been warnings and concerns about land issues before the violence, which deeply affected both communities.

She says leaders needed to pause, listen and engage in meaningful consultation when people expressed anger or raised concerns.

Kiran also stressed the importance of understanding iTaukei culture and sensitivities, saying the country needed greater engagement and dialogue.

She says democratic processes must be accompanied by genuine relationships with communities, including farmers and landowners, rather than one-sided engagement.

Kiran says the events of 2000 remained a lesson in the importance of listening to communities, recognising warning signs and ensuring people have systems they can turn to for protection.
